claim: High-throughput proteomic experiments often require high sample amounts and can be less sensitive compared to conventional proteomic experiments.
source: However, high-throughput proteomic experiments often require high sample amounts and can be less sensitive compared to conventional proteomic experiments.
evidence: This is stated as background context in the abstract without specific supporting data in this manuscript.

claim: Zeno SWATH MS is a data-independent acquisition technique that employs a linear ion trap pulsing (Zeno trap pulsing) to increase the sensitivity in high-throughput proteomic experiments.
source: Here, we introduce and benchmark Zeno SWATH MS, a data-independent acquisition technique that employs a linear ion trap pulsing (Zeno trap pulsing) to increase the sensitivity in high-throughput proteomic experiments.
evidence: This is the main methodological claim of the paper, supported by subsequent experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Using 20 min micro-flow-rate chromatography, Zeno SWATH MS identified more than 5000 proteins consistently from a 62.5 ng load of human cell line tryptic digest.
source: For instance, using 20 min micro-flow-rate chromatography, Zeno SWATH MS identified more than 5000 proteins consistently, and with a coefficient of variation of 6%, from a 62.5 ng load of human cell line tryptic digest.
evidence: Specific quantitative result from experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Zeno SWATH MS identified more than 5000 proteins with a coefficient of variation of 6% from a 62.5 ng load of human cell line tryptic digest using 20 min micro-flow-rate chromatography.

evidence: Specific quantitative result from experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Using 5 min analytical flow-rate chromatography (800 µl/min), Zeno SWATH MS identified 4907 proteins from a triplicate injection of 2 µg of a human cell lysate.
source: Using 5 min analytical flow-rate chromatography (800 µl/min), Zeno SWATH MS identified 4907 proteins from a triplicate injection of 2 µg of a human cell lysate, or more than 3000 proteins from a 250 ng tryptic digest.
evidence: Specific quantitative result from experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Using 5 min analytical flow-rate chromatography (800 µl/min), Zeno SWATH MS identified more than 3000 proteins from a 250 ng tryptic digest.
source: Using 5 min analytical flow-rate chromatography (800 µl/min), Zeno SWATH MS identified 4907 proteins from a triplicate injection of 2 µg of a human cell lysate, or more than 3000 proteins from a 250 ng tryptic digest.
evidence: Specific quantitative result from experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The proteome consists of large numbers of proteins that differ in concentration, distribution, and temporal dynamics.
source: The proteome consists of large numbers of proteins that differ in concentration, distribution, and temporal dynamics (Eriksson and Fenyö, 2007; Hixson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Data-dependent acquisition (DDA) selects precursors from full-scan MS1 mass spectrum for fragmentation, generating tandem (MS/MS or MS2) mass spectra that can be matched to spectra in a database.
source: In bottom-up proteomics, data-dependent acquisition (DDA) selects precursors from full-scan MS1 mass spectrum for fragmentation, generating tandem (MS/MS or MS2) mass spectra that can be matched to spectra in a database.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DDA methodology in proteomics.

claim: DDA can result in high numbers of missing values that can originate from the stochastic nature of precursors selected for fragmentation, which limits the application in high-throughput studies.
source: While DDA ensures selectivity, it can result in high numbers of missing values that can originate from, for example, the stochastic nature of precursors selected for fragmentation, which limits the application in high-throughput studies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about limitations of DDA in proteomics.

claim: Data-independent acquisition (DIA) techniques such as SWATH acquisition generate fragment ion spectra from all precursor ions that fall within a predefined precursor m/z range window.
source: Data-independent acquisition (DIA) techniques such as SWATH acquisition (Gillet et al., 2012) address this problem by generating fragment ion spectra from all precursor ions that fall within a predefined precursor m/z range window.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DIA methodology, supported by citation.

claim: DIA methods have facilitated applications in large-scale proteomics, including systems biology studies in various model organisms, disease states, and species.
source: DIA methods have facilitated applications in large-scale proteomics, including systems biology studies in various model organisms, disease states, and species (Hou et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2017; Basak et al., 2015; Zelezniak et al., 2018; Grobbler et al., 2015; Gillet et al., 2012), with one of the most common clinical applications being the discovery of (compound) biomarkers for disease in body fluids, particularly blood serum or plasma (Anjo et al., 2017; Gajbhiye et al., 2016; Russell et al., 2016; Hou et al., 2015; Pires et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: One of the most common clinical applications of DIA is the discovery of (compound) biomarkers for disease in body fluids, particularly blood serum or plasma.
source: DIA methods have facilitated applications in large-scale proteomics, including systems biology studies in various model organisms, disease states, and species (Hou et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2017; Basak et al., 2015; Zelezniak et al., 2018; Grobbler et al., 2015; Gillet et al., 2012), with one of the most common clinical applications being the discovery of (compound) biomarkers for disease in body fluids, particularly blood serum or plasma (Anjo et al., 2017; Gajbhiye et al., 2016; Russell et al., 2016; Hou et al., 2015; Pires et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Nano-flow chromatography is highly sensitive as sample dilution is minimal.
source: Proteomics has historically relied on nano-flow chromatography, which is highly sensitive as sample dilution is minimal (Muntel et al., 2019), but the low flow rate requires a longer gradient time, which is more susceptible to technical distortions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The low flow rate of nano-flow chromatography requires a longer gradient time, which is more susceptible to technical distortions.
source: Proteomics has historically relied on nano-flow chromatography, which is highly sensitive as sample dilution is minimal (Muntel et al., 2019), but the low flow rate requires a longer gradient time, which is more susceptible to technical distortions.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the properties of nano-flow chromatography.

claim: Columns compatible with nano-LC systems typically require exchange after a maximum of a few hundred injections.
source: Moreover, columns compatible with nano-LC systems typically require exchange after a maximum of a few hundred injections, which together prolongs the acquisition time and leads to complex batch effects in larger studies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about nano-LC systems.

claim: Recent advances in instrumentation and software have facilitated the use of faster gradients and higher chromatographic flow rates.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Faster gradients and higher chromatographic flow rates accelerate proteomic experiments and allow highly precise measurements.
source: These accelerate proteomic experiments and allow highly precise measurements.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the advances mentioned, supported by the preceding citations.

claim: Faster gradients and higher chromatographic flow rates come at the cost of a higher sample amount required and can yield lower proteomic depth.
source: These come, however, at the cost of a higher sample amount required and can yield lower proteomic depth.
evidence: This is stated as a trade-off of using faster gradients and higher flow rates.

claim: The sensitivity of SWATH MS in time-of-flight (TOF) mass spectrometers is largely determined by the MS/MS duty cycle.
source: The sensitivity of SWATH MS in time-of-flight (TOF) mass spectrometers is largely determined by the MS/MS duty cycle.
evidence: This is stated as technical knowledge about TOF mass spectrometers.

claim: The pulse in the TOF accelerator results in a duty cycle of TOFs of only 5–25%.
source: The pulse in the TOF accelerator, which results in a small proportion of ions situated at the right position of entering TOF, has a disproportionate impact on lower-m/z ions, resulting in a duty cycle of TOFs of only 5–25%.
evidence: This is stated as technical knowledge about TOF mass spectrometers.

claim: The Zeno trap allows all fragment ions to be trapped in an axial pseudopotential well and then released by potential energy with timing aligned to the next pulse at the accelerator, allowing a duty cycle increase, thus increasing intensity 4–20 times.
source: Here, we describe a setup of the Zeno trap (Loboda and Chernushevich, 2009; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), where all fragment ions are trapped in an axial pseudopotential well and then released by potential energy with timing aligned to the next pulse at the accelerator, allowing a duty cycle increase, thus increasing intensity 4–20 times (Baba et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to a figure showing the Zeno trap setup.
